summary: Extends SIP events so a subscriber can make a subscription conditional, avoiding notifications it has already received. The base framework offers no way to skip repeating notifications. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: You tell the news service to only send you news if something changed since your last copy.

questions: what is the sip suppress-if-match header
how to avoid duplicate sip notify
subtitle: Lets a SIP subscriber say 'only bother me if the state changed since the version I already have'.

tldr.problem: Every SIP SUBSCRIBE request, including refreshes, polls and unsubscribes, triggers a NOTIFY carrying the full current state, even when the subscriber already has it.
tldr.mechanism: The notifier tags each notification with an entity-tag in a SIP-ETag header field. The subscriber echoes the last tag in a Suppress-If-Match header field on later SUBSCRIBEs, and if it still matches, the notifier drops the body or the whole NOTIFY.
tldr.outcome: Redundant notifications are avoided for refreshes, polls, resumed subscriptions and unsubscribes. The mechanism is backward compatible, because unaware parties simply ignore the new header fields.

today: RFC 5839 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2010. According to the metadata for this entry it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Problem with Repeated Notifications
sections.content:
The SIP events framework lets a subscriber ask a notifier to report changes in some resource, such as presence or message waiting. Subscriptions have a finite lifetime set with the Expires header field, so they must be refreshed, typically every few minutes to hours depending on the event package.

By default every SUBSCRIBE generates a NOTIFY with the latest state. The same SUBSCRIBE method is used to start, refresh and end a subscription, and a zero-expiry SUBSCRIBE is a one-off fetch or poll. So the full state is resent on each refresh, poll or unsubscribe, even though the subscriber usually has it already. The RFC compares this with repeated HTTP GETs, which HTTP solves with conditional requests, and notes that SIP PUBLISH has a similar mechanism.

The RFC states five requirements. It must be possible to suppress the NOTIFY, or at least its body, when the subscriber already has the latest state. The mechanism must apply to resuming a paused subscription, refreshing, terminating, and fetching or polling.
sections.eli5: Each time you check in with the news service, it sends the whole story again even if nothing changed. That wastes everyone's time.

sections.title: Resources, Entities and Entity-Tags
sections.content:
A resource is an object identified by a URI whose state is accessed through SIP event notification. An entity is the representation of that state: the data in the NOTIFY body plus related header meta-data such as Content-Type, Content-Length and Event. A resource can have several entities, for example one per subscriber when each sees a filtered view. Each entity belongs to exactly one resource.

An entity has versions, of which one is current and the rest are stale. Each version is identified by an entity-tag, unique across all versions of all entities of one resource and event package. Whenever the body or any of the meta-data changes, the notifier MUST produce a new entity-tag. Subscription-State is explicitly not part of the entity.

Equal tags for different resources do not mean equal entities. With partial (delta) notifications, the tag applies to the full event state. Entity-tags are not expected to be shared with other mechanisms such as HTTP or PUBLISH unless an event package defines it.
sections.eli5: Each version of the news gets a ticket number. When the news changes, it gets a new ticket number, so a number tells you exactly which version you hold.

sections.title: How Conditional Notification Works
sections.content:
A notifier that supports the extension puts an entity-tag in a SIP-ETag header field of each NOTIFY. The subscriber stores the tag with the state. Later it adds a Suppress-If-Match header field to a SUBSCRIBE, containing the last tag it saw. The condition applies to the notifications that follow the SUBSCRIBE, not to the SUBSCRIBE itself, unlike If-Match in PUBLISH.

If the tag matches the notifier's current one, the condition is true. Outside an established dialog, the notifier MUST still send a NOTIFY but with no body (no Content-Type, Content-Length of zero), and with the unchanged tag. Inside an established dialog, the notifier MUST suppress the NOTIFY and answer the SUBSCRIBE with a 204 (No Notification) response. While the condition stays true, later NOTIFYs are also suppressed, except that if reportable header changes occur (such as Subscription-State), the notification is sent without a body. If the condition is false, normal behavior applies.

The special wildcard tag, a single asterisk, always matches. It effectively quenches a subscription, which is useful to put one in a dormant mode, for example to save bandwidth and power when the user is not watching contacts' presence.
sections.eli5: You tell the service 'I have ticket number ffee2'. If that is still the newest, it just says 'nothing new' instead of resending everything.

sections.title: Subscriber Procedures
sections.content:
A subscriber that wants to use the mechanism MUST store the entity-tag from each NOTIFY. When it builds a conditional SUBSCRIBE it MUST include a single conditional header field with one entity-tag, copied byte-wise from an earlier NOTIFY. It MUST NOT infer meaning from a tag's value, and MUST be ready to receive any tag value, even one it has seen before. If it gets a 204 to an in-dialog SUBSCRIBE, it MUST treat the event state and subscription state as unchanged.

  • Polling: send a zero-expiry SUBSCRIBE with the last tag. The notifier answers 202, then sends a NOTIFY with the same tag and no body if the state is unchanged.
  • Resuming: send a SUBSCRIBE with the last tag outside a dialog. If it is still valid, the first NOTIFY has no body. If not, the NOTIFY carries the latest state.
  • Refreshing: send the tag before expiry. On a match the notifier replies 204 with the new Expires and sends no NOTIFY.
  • Terminating: send the tag with Expires: 0. On a match the 204 concludes the subscription.

Support is detected implicitly. Unaware subscribers ignore the entity-tag, and unaware notifiers ignore the conditional header. The RFC adds a non-normative note that B2BUAs unaware of the mechanism may treat a body-less NOTIFY as an error. In that case subscribers should disable the feature and fall back to normal behavior.
sections.eli5: The reader keeps the last ticket number and shows it every time it checks in, whether starting again, renewing or quitting. If the number is still current, the answer is a quick 'nothing new'.

sections.title: Notifier Requirements
sections.content:
A notifier MUST generate entity-tags for all resources it is responsible for. The format is up to the notifier and opaque to the client; it can be any value except the single asterisk wildcard, for example a counter incremented per notification per resource. Each tag MUST map to one and only one presentation of resource state. The notifier MUST remember or be able to recompute the tag as long as that version is current. Tags used in PUBLISH are not necessarily shared with those used in subscriptions.

It MUST suppress only as the rules allow: it MUST NOT suppress a NOTIFY unless the SUBSCRIBE was sent in an established dialog, and a successful conditional SUBSCRIBE MUST extend the subscription expiry. Suppression never changes the resource's entity-tag.

For state differentials, the SIP-ETag MUST correspond to the full resource state. For list subscriptions (RFC 4662), the entity is the full state of the list including the Resource List Meta-Information documents and entity header.
sections.eli5: The service picks the ticket numbers however it likes, as long as each number means exactly one version. It must never skip your renewal when you show a good ticket.

sections.title: New Protocol Elements
sections.content:
The RFC adds one response code and two header fields. 204 (No Notification) means the request succeeded but the associated notification will not be sent; it is valid only in response to a SUBSCRIBE within an established dialog. SIP-ETag carries the entity-tag in notifications. Suppress-If-Match carries an entity-tag or the asterisk wildcard in a SUBSCRIBE; it may appear in any request, but its behavior is only defined for SUBSCRIBE.

The ABNF is Suppress-If-Match = "Suppress-If-Match" HCOLON ( entity-tag / "*" ), with entity-tag defined in RFC 3903. IANA registered the 204 code under Successful 2xx and the new header field name, both referring to RFC 5839.
sections.eli5: There is one new answer, 'done, but nothing will be sent', and a new line for showing your ticket number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the security considerations of SIP event notification are discussed in RFC 3265. This specification is an optimization that does not by itself alter the security properties of the protocol.
sections.eli5: This only saves repeat messages, so it does not make things safer or less safe.
